analysis.one_liner: Bars drug insurers and middlemen companies from also owning pharmacies.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have forced companies that sell insurance or manage drug benefits to sell their pharmacies, was introduced in the final week of the 118th Congress and died in committee without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for one company to both own a pharmacy and own a health insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager — the middlemen that negotiate drug prices and decide which pharmacies are in an insurer's network. Companies like CVS, which owns a drugstore chain, a large PBM, and an insurer, would have three years to sell off their pharmacies. Regulators could sue violators and force them to hand back pharmacy profits, with the money going to consumers who were overcharged.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent and community pharmacies, which compete against company-owned pharmacies that also control the networks deciding whether they get customers. Patients benefit indirectly: when the company steering prescriptions also owns the pharmacy filling them, independent pharmacies can be squeezed on reimbursement and patients can be steered toward the owner's stores. Consumers could also receive money recovered from companies found to have overcharged them at their own pharmacies.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it unlawful for any person to own or operate a pharmacy while also owning or operating a health insurance company or a pharmacy benefit manager, with a three-year deadline to divest the pharmacy [S2].

Federal health inspectors, the Justice Department's antitrust division, the FTC, and state attorneys general could sue violators, force divestiture, and make them disgorge pharmacy revenue earned during the violation [S2].
Any disgorged drug revenue would go into an FTC-run fund for the health needs of the harmed community, including consumers overcharged at vertically integrated pharmacies [S2].
The bill covers every pharmacy type, including mail-order, specialty, hospital, and long-term care pharmacies, so companies could not sidestep the ban by shifting the pharmacy's form [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Vertically integrated drug companies — chiefly the pharmacy chains that also own PBMs and insurers — would have to sell their pharmacy businesses within three years and could have to give back pharmacy revenue. Those companies argue the integrated model keeps costs down and that forced divestiture would disrupt service.

drawbacks.text: Forcing divestment within three years would be a massive corporate restructuring; if buyers cannot be found quickly, patients who rely on those pharmacies for convenience or specialty services could face disruption during the transition [S2].

The companies affected argue that owning pharmacies, PBMs, and insurers together lets them lower prices through scale and mail-order efficiency; a full ownership split would remove whatever savings that integration produced, and the bill does not itself cap drug prices or PBM fees.
Disgorgement of 'revenue' rather than proven overcharges is a blunt remedy; a company could owe back all prescription sales from a pharmacy it legally operated before the ban applied.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: breaking up companies that both steer prescriptions and fill them would protect independent pharmacies from a conflict of interest, but the transition would be disruptive and the bill does not guarantee drug prices fall — it removes one structural conflict rather than directly capping costs. The strongest cost is the abruptness of a three-year forced divestiture across a huge, intertwined industry; the strongest benefit is that enforcement includes taking back revenue and giving it to overcharged consumers, not just a fine.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with only about three weeks left in the Congress, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and the session ended before any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-TN) introduced the bill with Rep. Jake Auchincloss (D-MA) on December 11, 2024 [S1].
Two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no other cosponsors signed on [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and took no further action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].
Because the Congress ended, the bill died and would have to be reintroduced from scratch in the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that own pharmacies together with PBMs and insurers — most notably CVS Health — keep their integrated structure and pharmacy revenue, because nothing was enacted.

for.name: Rep. Diana Harshbarger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 11, 2024 and referred it to the Judiciary Committee.

for.name: Rep. Jake Auchincloss
for.what_they_did: Joined the Republican sponsor in introducing the bill across party lines.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup was scheduled before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican sponsor with a Democratic original cosponsor and two Democratic cosponsors — but the bill drew almost no cosupport and never reached a vote, so no partisan split was ever tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Vertically integrated pharmacy chains that also own PBMs and insurers (CVS, UnitedHealth/OptumRx, Cigna/Evernorth)
industries.note: The bill strikes directly at their business model: these companies both decide which pharmacies patients use and own the pharmacies that fill the prescriptions, and they would have to divest their pharmacies or give up the PBM/insurance side. Their gain from integration — capturing the prescription at every step — comes at the expense of independent pharmacies and, the bill argues, consumers who are steered and overcharged.

Independent pharmacies currently compete against rivals that own the PBM deciding reimbursement rates and network access; separating ownership would remove that conflict and improve their standing with patients.

PBMs that do not own pharmacies could keep operating, but the largest ones sit inside companies that also own pharmacies, so the practical effect is a forced choice between the PBM business and the pharmacy business.
